blocks.text: A timing report says that an algorithm took one millisecond. Without the input size, distribution, machine, build mode, and operation being timed, that number is almost uninterpretable. Complexity analysis supplies a different kind of evidence: how a chosen measure of work grows as the problem grows. It does not require pretending that every instruction costs the same on real hardware.

blocks.text: In this chapter, keep an operation ledger before using a clock. Count comparisons, moved elements, and additional storage separately. A search that performs fewer comparisons may still lose for a tiny dataset; a structure with excellent average throughput may still pause during reallocation. The point is to make those tradeoffs explicit rather than collapse them into one adjective such as “fast.”

topics.title: 2.1.1 Interpreting Big-O Notation
topics.summary: A linear scan can examine every one of n elements, giving O(n) comparisons in its worst case. A lower-bound search on an indexed sorted sequence halves an interval, giving O(log n) comparisons. A nested all-pairs loop often produces O(n squared), while a constant amount of work independent of n is O(1).

blocks.text: Big-O expresses an eventual upper bound. Saying that a work count T(n) is O(g(n)) means there are fixed positive constants and a starting size after which T(n) does not exceed a constant multiple of g(n). It does not say that the two functions are equal, that every input takes that much work, or that the hidden constant is small.

topics.title: 2.1.2 Comparing Common Growth Rates
topics.summary: Common growth rates separate dramatically as n increases: constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic, and exponential. For example, doubling n roughly doubles linear work, quadruples quadratic work, and adds about one halving step to a binary search.

blocks.text: A sorting prerequisite must be counted when comparing searches over originally unsorted data. Sorting once and performing many queries is a different workload from sorting before each single query. Likewise, an index can trade memory and update cost for lookup speed. The complete operation sequence determines which complexity comparison is relevant.

blocks.text: Common growth classes describe different responses to scale. Constant work does not grow with the number of stored elements. Logarithmic work grows by roughly one step when an ordered search space doubles. Linear work roughly doubles with the input. Linearithmic work adds a logarithmic factor, while quadratic work roughly quadruples when the input doubles. These are statements about models, not exact wall-clock ratios.

blocks.text: Derive a logarithmic count by repeated halving. Starting from 1024 candidates, the possible interval sizes can shrink through 512, 256, and so on toward one and zero. The number of halvings grows with the base-two logarithm. An extra comparison at a boundary explains why a particular implementation may perform eleven comparisons rather than the memorable number ten. The asymptotic statement tolerates a constant difference; a fixture checking exact output cannot ignore it.

blocks.text: For nested loops, inspect the bounds instead of multiplying mechanically. Two independent full scans nested together perform n*n visits. But a loop whose inner limit is the outer index visits 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) pairs, or n(n-1)/2. Both are quadratic, yet the exact formulas differ. Two consecutive loops add costs and remain linear; their indentation does not create a product.

blocks.text: Exponential growth is a warning about the size of a search space, not evidence that every recursive function is exponential. A recursion making one call on half the input behaves very differently from a recursion branching into two overlapping subproblems of almost the same size. Chapters 17 and 19 separate a search tree from a graph of repeated states.

blocks.text: Check storage as well as time. A dense V by V matrix has a quadratic number of cells even if one query is constant time. At one thousand vertices there are one million cells; at one hundred thousand there are ten billion. Before multiplying by bytes per cell, validate that the multiplication itself is representable. A complexity estimate becomes an engineering decision only when connected to an actual resource budget.

blocks.text: Best, average, and worst cases quantify different sets of inputs of the same size. In linear search, a first-element match needs one equality test. A missing value requires inspecting the whole sequence. An average claim requires a distribution: how likely is each position, and how often is the key absent? Without that information, “average” is an unstated guess.

blocks.text: Under the illustrative assumption that a present key is equally likely to be at each of n distinct positions, successful linear search uses an average of (n+1)/2 comparisons. That result follows from averaging one through n. It is not the average for a cache of frequently requested items deliberately kept at the front, nor for workloads dominated by missing keys. Change the workload and the average changes.

blocks.text: Worst-case analysis is not necessarily pessimism. A service accepting externally chosen keys may need a response-time bound even when common requests are cheap. A hash table’s expected behavior relies on distribution and load assumptions; a degenerate collision pattern can change its cost. A balanced search tree offers a different set of guarantees. Chapter 7 makes the collision mechanism visible before promising a constant-time lookup.

blocks.text: Distinguish a worst-case input from a worst-case machine event. Complexity can bound the number of comparisons while the operating system preempts the process or the allocator waits for memory. These environmental effects matter for latency but are not captured by the simple comparison model. Book VI will address timing requirements more directly; here the goal is to avoid claiming that an asymptotic bound is a deadline guarantee.

blocks.text: Tests should identify which case they exercise. A benchmark that repeatedly searches for the first element is not representative evidence for unsuccessful lookups. Likewise, a sort measured only on ascending data says little about a pivot rule vulnerable to another arrangement. Label datasets and preserve their construction so another engineer can reproduce the case rather than infer it from a graph title.

Under the illustrative assumption that a present key is equally likely to be at each of n distinct positions, successful linear search uses an average of (n+1)/2 comparisons. That result follows from averaging one through n. It is not the average for a cache of frequently requested items deliberately kept at the front, nor for workloads dominated by missing keys. Change the workload and the average changes.

Worst-case analysis is not necessarily pessimism. A service accepting externally chosen keys may need a response-time bound even when common requests are cheap. A hash table’s expected behavior relies on distribution and load assumptions; a degenerate collision pattern can change its cost. A balanced search tree offers a different set of guarantees. Chapter 7 makes the collision mechanism visible before promising a constant-time lookup.

Distinguish a worst-case input from a worst-case machine event. Complexity can bound the number of comparisons while the operating system preempts the process or the allocator waits for memory. These environmental effects matter for latency but are not captured by the simple comparison model. Book VI will address timing requirements more directly; here the goal is to avoid claiming that an asymptotic bound is a deadline guarantee.

Tests should identify which case they exercise. A benchmark that repeatedly searches for the first element is not representative evidence for unsuccessful lookups. Likewise, a sort measured only on ascending data says little about a pivot rule vulnerable to another arrangement. Label datasets and preserve their construction so another engineer can reproduce the case rather than infer it from a graph title.

topics.summary: The program compares two search mechanisms on the same sorted vector. It does not time them. The linear routine counts equality comparisons until a match or the end. The binary routine counts comparisons with the middle element while maintaining a candidate interval. The chosen missing key is below all stored values, making the behavior easy to trace by hand.

The correct comparison is between complete workflows with the same contract.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Is O(n) an exact elapsed-time promise? No. Does amortized constant append mean every append is constant work? No. Can two consecutive linear loops be quadratic merely because there are two? No; their counts add. Can a logarithmic number of comparisons coexist with linear traversal steps? Yes, when the representation lacks random access. This last distinction will matter when searching linked structures.
